cards.heading: Why automate
cards.body: Configuring devices one by one by hand is slow and error-prone, and configurations drift apart over time. Automation applies tested changes consistently and quickly to many devices, checks compliance, and frees engineers from repetitive work. The cost: you need skills in programming, APIs and tools. It's most valuable for repetitive changes across many devices, such as pushing a new NTP server to 500 switches in minutes. Configuration drift means configurations slowly diverging from the standard; automation tools compare devices with the intended state and correct the differences. The risk: a bad automated change spreads just as fast.

cards.heading: Three planes
cards.body: The data plane forwards traffic (switching frames, routing packets, applying ACLs). The control plane builds the information needed to forward: routing protocols, STP, ARP. The management plane is how people and tools manage the device: SSH, SNMP, APIs.

cards.heading: Traditional networks
cards.body: Every device runs its own control plane and is configured individually, box by box, usually through the CLI. Network-wide changes mean touching every device.

cards.heading: Controller-based networks
cards.body: An SDN controller centralises (some of) the control plane and the network's configuration. Devices keep the data plane. Administrators and applications work with the controller instead of individual boxes. The controller holds the central, network-wide view and policy, and programs the devices through its southbound interfaces.
cards.example:
Apps / scripts
             │  northbound API (REST)
        [ SDN controller ]
             │  southbound API (NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, CLI)
   [switch]  [switch]  [router]

cards.heading: Northbound and southbound
cards.body: The northbound interface (NBI) faces up, to applications and engineers, usually a REST API returning JSON. The southbound interface (SBI) faces down, to the devices: NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, or plain SSH/CLI.

cards.heading: Software-Defined Access
cards.body: Cisco SD-Access is a controller-based campus run from Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center). The underlay is the physical network of routed links (IS-IS). The overlay is built on top: VXLAN tunnels carry traffic, LISP acts as the control plane, and Cisco TrustSec group tags apply policy. Together they form the fabric. LISP's map server keeps endpoint-to-location mappings, so fabric nodes ask it where to tunnel traffic. Fabric edge nodes connect endpoints, much like access switches; border nodes connect to outside networks; control-plane nodes hold the LISP map server. Scalable group tags (SGTs) put endpoints into groups, and policy says which groups may talk, wherever the endpoints are, instead of using IP addresses.

cards.heading: Catalyst Center and traditional management
cards.body: Catalyst Center adds intent-based management: you describe the desired policy and it configures the devices. It also offers assurance (health scores, path traces, issue detection), software image management and a REST API for automation, compared with traditional device-by-device CLI management. Intent-based networking means stating the outcome you want (for example 'guests can't reach finance'); the controller translates it into configuration, deploys it and verifies the network behaves that way. Assurance turns streaming telemetry, logs and events into health scores, issues and guided fixes.

cards.heading: NETCONF, RESTCONF and YANG
cards.body: YANG is a data model language that describes a device's configuration and state. NETCONF carries YANG-modelled data encoded in XML over SSH, on port 830. RESTCONF offers the same YANG data over HTTPS, in JSON or XML, mapping HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) onto it. Both are southbound interfaces.
cards.example:
NETCONF   SSH port 830   XML
RESTCONF  HTTPS          JSON or XML
cards.mnemonic:
NETCONF rides SSH on port 830: "configure at 8:30 before the network gets busy". It speaks XML only.
RESTCONF is REST, so it uses HTTPS like any web API and adds JSON.
YANG is the what (the model), and NETCONF and RESTCONF are the how (the transport).
